lead: Machine design is the route from a need to a drawing that a workshop can make, inspect and sell. A need appears (a workshop must hang a ceiling fan from a brick wall, a pump maker needs a shaft that survives a restart after a Chennai power cut) and the designer turns it into sizes, materials, tolerances and a cost. The route is a loop, not a line: every stage can send the team back a step, and a fault found on paper costs a pencil stroke while the same fault found in the field costs a recall. Every stage balances function, strength, cost and ease of making.

blocks.text: Design starts with a need, not a formula. Someone wants a part that does a job at a price: transmit 5 kW at 900 rpm for ten years, for under ₹4,000. Some syllabi call this topic the introduction to the design process; most list the same stages.

items: Recognition of need: a customer, a market survey or a breakdown report shows a job done badly or at high cost.
Specification: the need becomes numbers: function, load, speed, life, size limits, cost ceiling and the codes to follow.
Synthesis (concept): two or three working principles or mechanisms are sketched and compared. Most of the final cost is fixed here.
Analysis of forces: the force, moment or torque on each element is found from the mechanism and its duty.
Selection of material and design of elements: each part gets a material, then its sizes from the stress and deflection checks.
Modification: sizes are rounded to standard values and changed for manufacture, assembly, appearance and cost.
Detailed drawing and prototype test: every dimension, tolerance and surface finish is frozen; one or a few pieces are built and measured.
Production: drawings, process sheets and inspection plans go to the shop floor.

blocks.text: Figure 1.1.1 draws this order with the feedback arrows that make it a loop. A prototype that cracks, a cost that overshoots the ceiling or a welder who cannot make the chosen joint sends the team back, sometimes to the concept, sometimes only to the detail. Returning early is cheap; returning after the tooling is cut is very costly. Good teams therefore test the risky idea first.
Nothing in a design is free. A change that makes a part stronger often makes it heavier, costlier or harder to make, so the design is the balance struck between these factors.

blocks.text: C is the cost per piece (₹). C<sub>mat</sub>, C<sub>mach</sub>, C<sub>weld</sub> and C<sub>over</sub> are the material, machining, welding and overhead (rent, power, supervision, inspection) charges per piece (₹). C<sub>setup</sub> is the one-time cost of a pattern, die or jig (₹), and N is the number of pieces made. Only the last term is divided by N.

The division by N is why the batch size changes the answer. A ₹60,000 casting pattern adds ₹300 per piece when N = 200 and only ₹12 when N = 5,000. So casting wins in large batches, while fabrication from bar or rolled sections, which needs only a cheap jig, wins in small ones.

sections.h3: The specification is the exit from the loop

blocks.text: A loop with no exit is churn. The specification is the exit: every revision is judged against the same written targets, so the team knows when to stop. It states the function in numbers (carry 8 kg, deflect less than 2 mm, last 5 years), the limits (envelope, mass, cost, codes), and how each target will be verified: a calculation, a bench test or inspection of the first piece.

The later chapters of this unit supply the tools for the analysis and detail stages: how loads vary with time (static, dynamic and impact loads), the stress equations, and the strength and stiffness checks.

examples.question: A small workshop in Chennai must supply wall brackets for an 8 kg ceiling fan. The bracket must last 5 years, the order is 200 pieces, the shop has manual milling and arc welding, and the selling price is ₹250 per bracket. (a) List the design stages for this bracket. (b) Find the dead load in newtons. (c) Per bracket, material costs ₹105, machining ₹55, welding ₹40 and overhead ₹30, and a drilling jig costs ₹2,000 once. Find the cost per bracket, the margin per bracket and the profit on the order.
steps: Need: a fan must hang safely from a brick wall for 5 years. Specification: mass 8 kg, life 5 years, 200 pieces, ₹250 each, mild vibration, coastal air.

Concept: compare a bent flat bar, a rolled angle and a welded T. Analysis and detail: pick the angle, fix its section, the bolt holes, the weld size and the paint. Prototype: hang one bracket with 8 kg, measure the deflection and shake it. Production: drawing, jig, first-piece inspection.
Dead load: W = m × g = 8 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 78.48 N. Here m is the fan mass and g = 9.81 m/s². This force, not the 8 kg, goes into every later stress formula.
Jig share per bracket: C<sub>setup</sub>/N = 2000/200 = ₹10. Cost per bracket C = 230 + 10 = ₹240.
Margin per bracket: 250 − 240 = ₹10. Order value: 200 × 250 = ₹50,000; profit: 200 × 10 = ₹2,000.
examples.answer: Dead load 78.48 N; cost ₹240 per bracket (₹230 direct plus ₹10 jig share); margin ₹10 per bracket, ₹2,000 on an order worth ₹50,000.

examples.question: The same bracket could be cast instead. A pattern costs ₹60,000 once, and a cast bracket then costs ₹120 to cast, machine and finish. The fabricated bracket of the first example costs ₹230 per piece plus a ₹2,000 jig. Find the batch size above which casting is cheaper, and the cost per piece of each route at 200 and 5,000 pieces.
steps: Total cost of N cast brackets: 60,000 + 120N. Total cost of N fabricated brackets: 2,000 + 230N.
Break-even when the totals are equal: 60,000 + 120N = 2,000 + 230N, so 110N = 58,000 and N = 527.3. Casting is cheaper from 528 pieces up.
At N = 200: cast 120 + 60,000/200 = ₹420; fabricated 230 + 2,000/200 = ₹240. Fabrication wins.
At N = 5,000: cast 120 + 60,000/5,000 = ₹132; fabricated 230 + 2,000/5,000 = ₹230.40. Casting wins by about ₹98 a piece.
examples.answer: Break-even at about 528 pieces. For the 200-piece order fabrication (₹240) beats casting (₹420); at 5,000 pieces casting (₹132) beats fabrication (₹230.40).

traps: Drawing the stages as a straight line. An answer that shows the feedback arrows (test back to concept, cost back to detail) scores more.
Assuming the stronger material is always better. Stiffness, mass, weldability and cost usually decide, not ultimate strength.
Calling the stress calculation "the design". It is one step, the design of elements, inside a longer procedure.
Dividing the whole cost by the batch size. Only the one-time setup cost is shared over N pieces; material and machining are paid on every piece.
Mixing mass and weight: 8 kg is a mass; the load is 78.48 N.

quiz.q: List the stages of the general design procedure in order.
quiz.a: Recognition of need, specification, synthesis (concept), analysis of forces, selection of material, design of elements, modification, detailed drawing and prototype test, production.

quiz.q: Name six factors that influence machine design.
quiz.a: Any six of: type of load and stresses, kinematics, material, form and size, use of standard parts, workshop facilities, number to be made, cost, safety, environment, maintenance, ergonomics and appearance.

quiz.q: Why does a prototype test often send a team backwards rather than forwards?
quiz.a: The prototype is the first physical evidence. It exposes wrong assumptions about load, material, weld quality or cost that paper could not show, so the concept or the detail sizes must be revised before release.

quiz.q: Why is most of the product cost fixed at the concept stage?
quiz.a: The concept fixes the working principle, the material family and the process (casting, forging or fabrication). Those set the floor on the cost per piece; later detail work only trims around it.

quiz.q: An order is 500 pieces at ₹180 each. Material is ₹70, machining ₹50, welding ₹25 and overhead ₹20 per piece, and a jig costs ₹4,000 once. Find the cost per piece and the margin.
quiz.a: Direct cost 70 + 50 + 25 + 20 = ₹165. Jig share 4000/500 = ₹8. Cost ₹173 per piece, margin 180 − 173 = ₹7.

quiz.q: A ceiling fan of mass 12 kg hangs from a bracket. Find the dead load, with g = 9.81 m/s².
A bracket designed for a dry inland town is sold in coastal Chennai. Which factors were under-weighted, and what two changes would you make?
quiz.a: Environment and maintenance. Specify galvanising or a zinc-rich paint, and remove crevices where salt water collects so the joint stays easy to inspect.

beyond: Industry runs this loop with CAD models, simulation and product lifecycle management software, so the specification, the drawing and the test record stay tied to one revision number. Design for manufacture and assembly (DFMA) pushes the shop floor's limits into the concept stage, and value engineering asks what each feature costs against what it does. Search next for DFMA, value engineering and product lifecycle management.
